Diabetes Regression: Final Comprehensive Analysis

Kosbay Assylzhan, Azatkyzy Arailym, Bolatkazy Togzhan, Mussamatova Zhasmina

2025-12-15

Introduction

Research Problem:

We aim to predict disease progression (target) in diabetes patients (\(n = 442\)) using 10 baseline physiological variables. This report follows a structured approach: EDA, Modeling, Diagnostics (including outlier removal), and Final Validation.

Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)

We start by loading the data and examining the structure of variables.

Graphical Displays

Distribution of All Variables

We visualize the histograms of all 10 predictors and the target variable to check for skewness and distribution shapes.

df %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = everything(), names_to = "Variable", values_to = "Value") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Value)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "#2c3e50", color = "white", bins = 20) +
  facet_wrap(~Variable, scales = "free") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Distributions of All Variables", y = "Count")

Linear Relationships (scatter plots)

We visualize the linear relationship between every predictor \(X\) and the target variable \(Y\).

df %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = -target, names_to = "Predictor", values_to = "Value") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Value, y = target)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3, color = "#2980b9") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "#c0392b", se = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~Predictor, scales = "free_x", ncol = 3) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(title = "Linear Relationship: Predictors vs Target")

Outlier Detection (Standardized Boxplots)

We transform the data into Z-scores (standard deviations from the mean) to visualize potential outliers across all variables simultaneously. Points colored in red or lying beyond the dashed lines (\(Z > 3\) or \(Z < -3\)) represent extreme values that may distort the model.

df %>%
  scale() %>% 
  as.data.frame() %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = everything(), names_to = "Variable", values_to = "Z_Score") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Variable, y = Z_Score, fill = Variable)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.6, outlier.colour = "red", outlier.shape = 8) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(-3, 3), linetype="dashed", color="gray") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Outlier Detection: Scaled Boxplots", y = "Z-Score") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

Correlation Matrix & Multicollinearity Check

We compute the correlation matrix to quantify the linear relationships between variables. We are particularly interested in multicollinearity — when two predictor variables are highly correlated (e.g., coefficient \(> 0.8\)). This can make the model unstable.

M <- cor(df)
corrplot(M, method = "color", type = "lower", order = "hclust",
         tl.col = "black", tl.cex = 0.8, addCoef.col = "black", number.cex=0.6)

Modeling

Initial Model Comparison (Full vs. EDA vs. Stepwise)

Before performing outlier cleaning, we evaluate three candidate model specifications on the original dataset to understand the baseline performance.

  1. Full Model: Includes all 10 predictors.
  2. EDA Model: Includes variables selected based on visual inspection (bmi, bp, s3, s5, s6).
  3. Stepwise Model: Uses AIC to automatically select the best subset of variables.
# 1. Full Model 
full_model <- lm(target ~ ., data = df)

# 2. EDA-based Model 
model_eda <- lm(target ~ bmi + bp + s3 + s5 + s6, data = df)

# 3. Stepwise Model
model_step <- stepAIC(full_model, direction = "both", trace = FALSE)

summary(full_model)
##

## lm(formula = target ~ ., data = df)
## 
## Residuals:
##      Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max

## Coefficients:

## Multiple R-squared:  0.5177, Adjusted R-squared:  0.5066 
## F-statistic: 46.27 on 10 and 431 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16
# Adjusted R-squared
adj_r2_full <- summary(full_model)$adj.r.squared
adj_r2_eda  <- summary(model_eda)$adj.r.squared
adj_r2_step <- summary(model_step)$adj.r.squared

# AIC
aic_full <- AIC(full_model)
aic_eda  <- AIC(model_eda)
aic_step <- AIC(model_step)

# RMSE
rmse_full <- rmse(df$target, predict(full_model, df))
rmse_eda  <- rmse(df$target, predict(model_eda, df))
rmse_step <- rmse(df$target, predict(model_step, df))

# Display Comparison
comparison_df <- data.frame(
  Model = c("Full Model", "EDA Model", "Stepwise Model"),
  Adj_R2 = c(adj_r2_full, adj_r2_eda, adj_r2_step),
  AIC = c(aic_full, aic_eda, aic_step),
  RMSE = c(rmse_full, rmse_eda, rmse_step)
)

Outlier Detection (Cook’s Distance)

Based on the initial analysis, the Full Model allows us to detect outliers across the entire feature space. We use Cook’s Distance to identify influential data points. We use the standard threshold of \(4/n\) (indicated by the red dashed line).

cooksD <- cooks.distance(full_model)
n <- nrow(df)
cutoff <- 4/n 

plot(cooksD, pch = 20, main = "Influential Obs by Cook's Distance", ylab="Cook's Distance")
abline(h = cutoff, col = "red", lty = 2)
text(x=1:length(cooksD)+1, y=cooksD, labels=ifelse(cooksD>cutoff, names(cooksD),""), col="red", cex=0.6, pos=3)

Action: Removing Outliers & Refitting

Decision: We identified and removed observations that exceeded the Cook’s Distance threshold (\(4/n\)).

Justification: These points represent approximately 5% of the dataset. While excluding data requires caution, these observations exhibited disproportionate influence on the regression coefficients. They likely represent clinical anomalies or potential data entry errors.

We create a cleaned dataset df_clean and refit the model.

influential_obs <- as.numeric(names(cooksD)[(cooksD > cutoff)])

# 2. Creating cleaned dataset 'df_clean'
df_clean <- df[-influential_obs, ] 

# Building models on cleaned data for comparison
full_model_clean <- lm(target ~ ., data = df_clean)

# 3. Creating 'model_step_clean'
model_step_clean <- stepAIC(full_model_clean, direction="both", trace=FALSE)

cat("Observations identified as outliers:", length(influential_obs), "\n")
## Observations identified as outliers: 22
cat("Original Stepwise (model_step) Adj. R2:      ", summary(model_step)$adj.r.squared, "\n")
## Original Stepwise (model_step) Adj. R2:       0.5081925
cat("Cleaned Stepwise (model_step_clean) Adj. R2: ", summary(model_step_clean)$adj.r.squared, "\n")
## Cleaned Stepwise (model_step_clean) Adj. R2:  0.5681814

Final Model Selection

We define our Final Model as the Stepwise model derived from the original dataset.

# Assigning 'model_step' (Original Data) as the Final Model
final_model <- model_step

Diagnostics of the Final Cleaned Model

We generate diagnostic plots for the final model to ensure that issues like non-normality or heteroscedasticity have been mitigated.

par(mfrow=c(2,2))
plot(final_model)

par(mfrow=c(1,1))

Format Statistical Tests

Visual diagnostics can sometimes be subjective. To rigorously verify the regression assumptions, we conduct formal statistical tests:

  • Shapiro-Wilk Test: Checks if residuals are normally distributed (\(H_0\): Normality holds).
  • Breusch-Pagan Test: Checks if the variance of residuals is constant (\(H_0\): Homoscedasticity holds).
shapiro.test(residuals(final_model))
## 
##  Shapiro-Wilk normality test
## 
## data:  residuals(final_model)
## W = 0.99724, p-value = 0.6719
bptest(final_model)
## 
##  studentized Breusch-Pagan test
## 
## data:  final_model
## BP = 21.908, df = 6, p-value = 0.001258

Addressing Heteroscedasticity: Log-Transformation Check

Since the Breusch-Pagan test might indicate heteroscedasticity, we check if a log-transformation improves the model assumptions.

# Create log-transformed target
df$log_target <- log(df$target)

log_model_full <- lm(log_target ~ . -target -log_target, data = df) # Exclude target and log_target from predictors
log_model_step <- stepAIC(log_model_full, direction="both", trace=0)

summary(log_model_step)
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = log_target ~ sex + bmi + bp + s1 + s2 + s5, data = df)
## 
## Residuals:
##      Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
## -1.63179 -0.24800  0.02884  0.28989  0.97557 
## 
## Coefficients:
##             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept)  4.88132    0.01922 253.992  < 2e-16 ***
## sex         -1.76757    0.44733  -3.951 9.06e-05 ***
## bmi          3.14035    0.49040   6.404 3.94e-10 ***
## bp           2.15254    0.46853   4.594 5.70e-06 ***
## s1          -6.37741    1.19899  -5.319 1.67e-07 ***
## s2           5.08346    1.09662   4.636 4.71e-06 ***
## s5           6.33442    0.59916  10.572  < 2e-16 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 0.404 on 435 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared:  0.484,  Adjusted R-squared:  0.4768 
## F-statistic: 67.99 on 6 and 435 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16
bp_test <- bptest(log_model_step)
cat(sprintf("Breusch-Pagan Test (Log-Model): BP = %.2f, p-value = %.5f\n", 
            bp_test$statistic, bp_test$p.value))
## Breusch-Pagan Test (Log-Model): BP = 14.73, p-value = 0.02245
# Shapiro-Wilk Test
sw_test <- shapiro.test(residuals(log_model_step))
cat(sprintf("Shapiro-Wilk Test (Log-Model): W = %.3f, p-value = %.5f\n", 
            sw_test$statistic, sw_test$p.value))
## Shapiro-Wilk Test (Log-Model): W = 0.983, p-value = 0.00006

Conclusion on Transformations

Based on the diagnostic tests, if the log-transformation does not significantly resolve heteroscedasticity or worsens normality, we choose to proceed with the linear model (on original data) for the final analysis for easier interpretation.

Model Validation (10-Fold Cross-Validation)

To assess how well the model predicts new, unseen data, we perform 10-Fold Cross-Validation on our final model (using original data).

set.seed(123)

train_control <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10)

cv_model <- train(
  formula(model_step_clean),
  data = df_clean,
  method = "lm",
  trControl = train_control
)

cv_model

Final Model Equation & Interpretation

The final fitted regression equation (based on the stepwise model) is:

\[ \hat{Y} = \beta_0 + \beta_1(Sex) + \beta_2(BMI) + \beta_3(BP) + \beta_4(S1) + \beta_5(S2) + \beta_6(S5) \]

(Coefficients values can be read from the table above)

Interpretation of Key Predictors:

  • Intercept (\(\beta_0\)): The expected disease progression score when all standardized predictors are zero.
  • BMI (\(\beta_2\)): Holding all other variables constant, an increase in Body Mass Index is strongly positively associated with disease progression.
  • S5 (\(\beta_6\)): Represents Log of Serum Triglycerides. High triglyceride levels are a metabolic risk factor, which explains why this variable has the largest positive coefficient and is a strong driver of disease progression.
  • S1 (\(\beta_4\)) & S2 (\(\beta_5\)): S1 usually shows a negative effect while S2 shows a positive effect. This often happens due to high correlation between these blood serum markers.
  • Sex (\(\beta_1\)): Biological sex shows a significant negative association in this specific encoding.

All selected predictors are statistically significant (\(p < 0.001\)), confirming their importance in modeling diabetes progression.
